section_1.title: The Intuitive Bridge (0:00-0:45)
section_1.content: Review 'Geometric Vectors' (arrows in R²). Introduce the shift: what if the 'things' we add aren't just arrows, but functions or polynomials? Establish the prerequisite: familiarity with basic vector addition and scalar multiplication.
section_1.example: Visualizing an arrow on a 2D plane vs. a waveform (sine wave) that can also be stretched and added together.

section_2.title: Defining the Rules of the Game (0:45-2:00)
section_2.content: Introduce the 8 Axioms of a Vector Space. Use a graphical checklist animation: Closure, Associativity, Commutativity, Identity, and Inverses. Emphasize that a vector space is not the 'object' itself, but the 'behavior' of the set.
section_2.example: A 'Robot Arm' analogy: If the robot's movement options satisfy these 8 rules, they form a vector space, regardless of whether the movement is linear or rotational.

section_3.title: The Surprise: Polynomials as Vectors (2:00-3:30)
section_3.content: Show that the set of polynomials P₂ = {ax² + bx + c} satisfies the 8 axioms. Use a split-screen animation: left side shows arrows, right side shows a polynomial graph morphing as coefficients change, demonstrating that addition behaves exactly the same.
section_3.example: Representing a polynomial (x² + 2x + 1) as a 'vector' [1, 2, 1], proving we can perform linear algebra on abstract functions.

section_4.title: Visualizing Dimensions (3:30-4:30)
section_4.content: Explain that 'dimension' is the number of degrees of freedom. In P₂, you have three coefficients (x², x, and constant), so the dimension is 3, visually represented as a 3D coordinate system where each axis is a basis polynomial.
section_4.example: A digital synthesizer: 'Sound' parameters (frequency, amplitude, phase) acting as the basis vectors for a space of all possible sound waves.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Why it Matters (4:30-5:00)
section_5.content: Summarize that abstract vector spaces allow us to use the power of linear algebra (matrices, projections, eigenvectors) on data, images, and quantum states.
section_5.example: A cute character 'Vector the Dog' jumping between 'Arrow World' and 'Function World,' showing that the same math 'leash' controls both.

section_2.content: Introduce the 8 Axioms of a Vector Space. Use a graphical checklist animation: Closure, Associativity, Commutativity, Identity, and Inverses. Emphasize that a vector space is not the 'object' itself, but the 'behavior' of the set.
section_2.example: A 'Robot Arm' analogy: If the robot's movement options satisfy these 8 rules, they form a vector space, regardless of whether the movement is linear or rotational.

section_3.title: The Surprise: Polynomials as Vectors (2:00-3:30)
section_3.content: Show that the set of polynomials P₂ = {ax² + bx + c} satisfies the 8 axioms. Use a split-screen animation: left side shows arrows, right side shows a polynomial graph morphing as coefficients change, demonstrating that addition behaves exactly the same.
section_3.example: Representing a polynomial (x² + 2x + 1) as a 'vector' [1, 2, 1], proving we can perform linear algebra on abstract functions.

section_4.title: Visualizing Dimensions (3:30-4:30)
section_4.content: Explain that 'dimension' is the number of degrees of freedom. In P₂, you have three coefficients (x², x, and constant), so the dimension is 3, visually represented as a 3D coordinate system where each axis is a basis polynomial.
section_4.example: A digital synthesizer: 'Sound' parameters (frequency, amplitude, phase) acting as the basis vectors for a space of all possible sound waves.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Why it Matters (4:30-5:00)
section_5.content: Summarize that abstract vector spaces allow us to use the power of linear algebra (matrices, projections, eigenvectors) on data, images, and quantum states.
section_5.example: A cute character 'Vector the Dog' jumping between 'Arrow World' and 'Function World,' showing that the same math 'leash' controls both.

Polynomial coefficients define your basis.

Axes map to independent variable parameters.

One math language binds diverse systems.
